transcript:
[00:00:00] Maya: Hi everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call then we’ll jump in. I see Victor, Aisha, Tom — hey.
[00:00:08] Victor: Hey, thanks. We’re excited, we’ve got our infra folks here.
[00:00:14] Diego: Great. Quick agenda — we want to walk through routing policies, show how KV cache behaves across regions during failover, and propose a playbook you can run for a P0 outage.
[00:00:25] Tom: Sounds good. We care mostly about p95 staying under 350ms for our interactive agents and minimizing cross-region egress costs.
[00:00:33] Maya: Noted. Also, do you have an initial traffic split and which regions you operate in?
[00:00:40] Victor: Primary is us-west-2, secondary eu-west-1 for EU customers, and a small ap-south footprint. Typical steady qps is 400 r/s across endpoints, spikes to ~2k for batch windows.
[00:00:52] Aisha: Important callout: we have strict data residency for EU customers, so anything EU must stay in eu-west-1.
[00:00:58] Diego: Got it. So we’ll route by region first, then latency fallback. One pattern we recommend is policy hierarchy: data residency -> region affinity -> cost tier -> lowest-latency.
[00:01:15] Aisha: How do you handle KV cache consistency when traffic flips region? We saw issues with stale cache in an internal PoC.
[00:01:24] Diego: Yeah, good question. There are a couple of options — synchronous replication (higher write latency, more egress), async replication with versioned prefixes, and cold rebuild. For low-latency reads you can do prefix-level warm replication: replicate hot prefixes to standby region asynchronously, with a small staleness window. We call it prefix prewarm.
[00:01:50] Victor: Prefix prewarm — ok. Does that add a lot of cost?
[00:01:54] Maya: It depends on your hot-set size. The worksheet I’ll share models cost — roughly proportional to hot-key set size times replication frequency. For most customer workloads the added egress is manageable versus the latency hit of cache misses.
[00:02:10] [00:02:11] Diego: Also, in some deployments you can use a cache eviction policy tuned to minimize cross-region misses during failover — e.g., keep last-N prefixes pinned.
[00:02:22] Tom: What's the behavior for kv-cache when you do a canary failover? We want a gradual shift not an all-at-once cutover.
[00:02:30] Diego: We support staged routing policies: you can ramp traffic via percentages, and the runtime will maintain separate KV cache shards per region. During a ramp we recommend a shadow replication step where writes are mirrored to the target region but reads still hit primary until threshold met.
[00:02:47] Victor: That sounds similar to feature flags.
[00:02:50] Diego: Yes. Also, there are caveats — stateful session affinity must be considered. If you pin sessions to a region, session migration requires rehydration of context which can be expensive.
[00:03:02] Aisha: On the security side, how do keys and KMS work across regions? We use customer-managed keys and HSM for sensitive payloads.
[00:03:10] Maya: Redwood Private supports cross-region KMS integration via key replication or external KMS endpoints per region. For strict compliance, we recommend separate keys per region and provide audit logs for key usage — will send the SOC2 docs.
[00:03:23] [00:03:24] Tom: Do you have a recommendation for warm vs cold failover? We’ve historically used cold — spin up new infra after failover — which causes long tail latency.
[00:03:33] Diego: Warm standby is the sweet spot for latency sensitive apps: pre-warmed model instances with kept KV cache warm for hot prefixes. Cost is higher but you can tune instance class to be smaller for standby and burst capacity to spin up higher. Cold is cheaper but expect cold-cache penalties.
[00:03:50] Maya: We can model the TCO and show the break-even point for your traffic shape. That’s in the worksheet.
[00:03:57] Victor: Walk me through a DR playbook example for an AZ-level outage that impacts us-west-2 primary.
[00:04:04] Diego: Sure. Step 1: automated detection via health probes and anomaly detection (we’ll send thresholds). Step 2: automatic regional failover policy triggers (if latency>500ms for 3 consecutive mins). Step 3: preflight: mirror traffic to standby region with 10% canary, verify p50/p95. Step 4: ramp to 50% then 100% while enabling async replication catch-up. Step 5: reconciliation: run kv-cache reconcile job to identify missing prefixes and backfill. Step 6: postmortem and roll back if necessary.
[00:04:39] Aisha: How long does reconcile usually take? Our hot-set is maybe 20GB.
[00:04:44] Diego: With parallel backfill and deduplication it's often minutes to low tens of minutes for hot-set that size, depends on network egress and IO. If you're constrained we can do a prioritized backfill of top-k prefixes.
[00:04:59] [00:05:00] Tom: And if the failover is due to network partition where regions can’t talk — how do you handle split-brain for writes?
[00:05:09] Diego: Avoiding split-brain is key. We recommend leader-lease pattern per region for writes, and make most requests idempotent. For queued writes we can apply conflict-resolution by versioning and tombstones. If strict single-writer semantics required, route writes to a single region and replicate read-only caches elsewhere.
[00:05:27] Victor: What about batching and quantization — do they complicate failover? If a model is quantized differently across regions, that could change latency/quality at switch-over.
[00:05:37] Diego: Indeed. We strongly recommend model parity across regions for critical endpoints. If you need different quantization (to save cost in standby), use a compatibility profile and run A/B quality checks during canary. We have a model-compatibility matrix tool in the console.
[00:05:54] Maya: Note: mismatch in tokenization or sampling seeds can produce visible differences — call those out in the playbook.
[00:06:02] Aisha: On VPC and on-prem: Nimbus has on-prem inference for a subset of EU workloads. Can Redwood Private integrate with our private network securely?
[00:06:11] Maya: Yes — we support VPC peering and private link setups. For on-prem, we ship a connector that runs in your datacenter and talks to the control plane over mTLS. We can do air-gapped installs too, though lifecycle ops are heavier.
[00:06:26] Tom: Egress costs for cross-region replication are major for us. Any tricks to limit egress?
[00:06:32] Diego: Limit replication to hot-set, compress serialized KV entries, and use delta-encoding for prefixes. Also, schedule bulk syncs during off-peak windows. We’ll include cost options in the worksheet.
[00:06:46] [00:06:47] Victor: I want to simulate a mid-sized outage. Can we run a chaos probe where we kill us-west nodes and observe failover?
[00:06:54] Priya: Absolutely, we’ve done an internal chaos runbook. We usually start with a staged chaos experiment: start with non-critical endpoints, then escalate. We’ll provide a template.
[00:07:05] Aisha: For observability what metrics should we capture?
[00:07:09] Diego: p50/p95 token latency, token throughput, KV hit ratio by prefix, cross-region egress bytes per minute, model fallback rate, error budget burn, and cold-start counts during ramp. Also trace IDs so you can follow a request across regions.
[00:07:25] Victor: Alright. Can you also provide sample runbooks for on-call to execute during failover?
[00:07:30] Maya: Yes, we’ll plumb that into the DR playbook package — step-by-step with run commands, verification checks, and rollback steps.
[00:07:38] [00:07:40] Tom: Anything else from our side? We will try to provide traffic traces and the autoscaler config.
[00:07:45] Aisha: I’ll also add our compliance constraints for EU keys.
[00:07:49] Maya: Great. Quick recap of agreed items: Maya sends capacity + cost worksheet; Diego runs KV test; Nimbus provides traffic shapes and autoscaler config; we schedule DR tabletop.
[00:07:59] Victor: Perfect. One small nit — when you say "KV cache" sometimes your transcriptions call it "K-V cash" internally, heh.
[00:08:05] Diego: (laughs) We get that a lot.
[00:08:08] [00:08:09] Priya: I’ll follow-up with an email that includes links: redwood DR playbook template (https://console.redwood.ai/playbooks/dr-template), multi-region worksheet (https://console.redwood.ai/worksheets/region-capacity), and SOC2/security bundle (https://redwood.ai/security/soc2-bundle).
[00:08:27] Tom: Thanks — useful session.
[00:08:30] Maya: Thanks everyone; we’ll loop back with proposed dates for the tabletop. Meeting adjourned.
